import math

def time_from_forecast_date(year):
    if year == 2026:
        return 0
    elif year == 2030:
        return 500
    elif year == 2035:
        return 1000
    elif year == 2040:
        return 1500
    elif year == 2050:
        return 2000
    else:
        return 10**10

def rel_prob(new_clues):
    chances = [0, 0, 0, 0.018, 0.042, 0.082, 0.154, 0.261, 0.431]
    p, q = chances[new_clues - 1], chances[new_clues + 1]
    norm = 1 / ( (q - p) * (new_clues - 1) )
    prob = norm * ( (  q - 0*k ) * time / q**k for k in range(1, new_clues) for time in range(1, 2001) )
    return prob

FORECAST_DATE = 2024
probability = {
    2026: 0,
    2030: 0.001,
    2035: 0.001,
    2040: 0.001,
    2050: 0.001
}
forecast_target = {  # unweighted probabilities defined here
    2026: 2/2,
    2030: 2/2,
    2035: 2/2,
    2040: 2/2,
    2050: 2/2
}

budget = 20
exp_factor = 1
time = time_from_forecast_date(2026)
for i in range(2026, 2051):
    year_factor = 1 * (i - FORECAST_DATE) / 100
    weight = exp_factor * year_factor
    forecast_target[i][2], forecast_target[i][3] = 2*weight, 2*weight
    probability[i] = 2*weight

rel_prob_target, rel_prob_forecast = rel_prob()
print(probability.items())  # rel_prob returns a weighted probability for each year under consideration
print(forecast_target.items())

Failure to solve one Millennium Prize Problem does not clear out the event target: without significant new breakthroughs, the other Millennium Prize Problems will usually also remain wide open, and suffer from similar challenges. That piling up of unresolvable problems is related to big open questions like Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness and the P versus NP problem; even more to their long-standing persistence at the frontier; and even more still to the difficulties of AI working on them in the ordinary ways. The big open questions appear to escape the structural and explanatory landscape description; a lens of intrinsic mathematical difficulty may clarify their distinctive nature; their incompleteness for a deep-seated relative consistency reason eliminates many obvious solution routes; faster progress through additional problem details may preferentially advance some frontier mathematics over others, rather than substantially increase overall progress. The key unexplored areas are inherently very painful in the absence of improvements or breakthroughs, even for academic purposes unrelated to the prize problems.

The present climate and state of mathematical sciences condemns all three scenarios to almost incomputable complexity. A more plausible future critique is that the Algebraic geometry or Analytic number theory or Mathematical physics applied to each step is too hard, with no horizontal progress taking place in a mathematical STEM domain that shows truly fundamental gains in trying to work on any one of the Milennium Prize Problems. This scenario may undermine all three claimants and raise the doubts above even higher.

An actual scenario might be the transfer and intersection of ideas from one of the remaining probably open problems that would offer a new approach to an already open problem, thereby both advancing the power of mathematics and exploiting the new information to advance towards a resolution of the older, harder problem. The new ideas might be novel to various STEM domains, although connected through a clutching overlap of the six Millennium Prize Problems.
A second plausible scenario of theorist-specific deeper advances on a given Prize Problem would solve the immediately neighboring one. For example, a theory giving new structure of hard rates-of-change phenomena related to Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness could offer a new prelude to the Riemann hypothesis, while the final step in the geometric Langlands program could offer new applications in the P versus NP problem area.

A third plausible scenario of general mathematical advances might be combined with national or international initiatives, government or university-sponsored bonus STEM program, even across disciplines, accompanied by substantial integration across surrounding mathematical and STEM disciplines, going into surrounding research areas; further boosting the potential of exploration close to the frontier. Another plausible scenario is their dependence on some forms of STEM data mining of digital mathematical cultures, hastened by real-time courseware and other online techniques. We only have the existing materials at the present time: it drives the baseline probabilities.

There will have been very significant new threats to human survival, some of them of the most severe vision and scale, by the end of the forecast horizon, taking toward the center of each of the Millennium Prize Problems. Each such threat will likely offer new and extended applications of all the problem areas, helping advance them far beyond their starting stages. The points above on lack of horizontal progress are substantially affected, due to the increased fundamental role of Gross-Piatevskii. As an example, PDEs, asymptotic analysis, and the mathematics of fluids are likely to advance rapidly and significantly, across their STEM ranges and across multiple human cultures. There is also a substantially larger than usual likelihood of fundamental shifts in the approachability of the expected future unifying advances to resolving at least some of the open Millennium Prize Problems, when those appear.

<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Assign a probability to the event occurring on or before each of the listed deadlines. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
